author: skill agent (ADR-22)
subject_model: kimi (ADR-32 funded account) by default; a Claude run is the monthly OKR benchmark
judge: a model other than the subject; rubric tasks only

policy.subject: kimi-k2.6
policy.pre_registered: 2026-10-23, by the alexandria chair before either arm ran on this suite: no results.json has ever been written for it. The numbers copy the three suites that already registered them, so every suite in the library is measured under one policy. The first run is on qwen/qwen3.8-27b with the subject overridden on the command line and recorded in the result, because the host that can run it holds a Groq key and no Moonshot key, and the Modal workspace is at its spend limit.

note: Ten treatment tasks and two controls from the five cited papers (ADR-35). This skill's own strongest finding is that a hand-written skill can go net negative, so its eval is the one with the most at stake: if any suite in the library should be believed over its author, it is this one. Revised 2026-10-26 for the ADR-38 retrofit: `sections` repointed at the six delta headings, every rubric criterion tied to a certificate and every rubric task shipping an exploit that must score zero (ADR-40 item 5), two anchors restated against the re-read papers, and sle-t10 added as a hard check with no judge in it.

sections: Delta 1: write from recorded runs, and read the per-family number rather than the average
tasks.situation: GraphSkillEvo's baseline table, read in full on 2026-10-26: under the Codex harness with GPT-5.4, an expert-written skill averaged 67.23 and a description-written one 67.21 against a 67.97 no-skill baseline, while trajectory-grounded skills averaged 8.98 to 10.31 points above it. With no harness the same two sources were net positive, +2.14 and +2.13 on GPT-5.4 and +7.39 and +8.42 on GPT-5.4-nano, so the net-negative result is one configuration of three. What holds everywhere is the gap to grounded skills, and that SpreadsheetBench was negative for a hand-written skill in all three configurations.
tasks.prompt: Our agent handles supplier-invoice reconciliation and gets it wrong often enough that finance checks every result. Priya has done this job by hand for six years and knows every edge case. The plan is to sit with her for two days, write a SKILL.md capturing everything she knows about the task, and load it into the agent. She is available Thursday. Anything I should know before we start?
tasks.without_skill: Endorses the plan enthusiastically, because capturing expert knowledge into a document is what everyone believes skills are for, and offers a template and interview questions.
tasks.with_skill: Warns that an expert-written skill is measurably capable of making the agent worse, and reorders the work: run the task unaided first, keep the trajectories, and spend Priya's two days on what the runs actually got wrong.

criteria.criterion: States that a skill written from expertise or from the task description can leave the agent worse off than no skill at all.

anchors.1: Generic caution that skills need testing, or the net-negative result stated with no configuration attached, which is the overstatement this suite's own skill carried until 2026-10-26.
anchors.2: States the measured result with its configuration: under the Codex harness on GPT-5.4 an expert-written skill averaged 67.23 and a description-written one 67.21 against 67.97 for no skill, and on SpreadsheetBench a hand-written skill was net negative in all three published configurations, costing 7.5 points in the worst of them.

certificate.names: the 67.23 and 67.21 averages against the 67.97 no-skill baseline under the Codex harness on GPT-5.4, and the -7.50 SpreadsheetBench row

criteria.criterion: Puts unaided runs before the writing, and makes the trajectories the input.

anchors.2: Run the task with no skill loaded, keep the trajectories, then write from the recorded failures.

certificate.names: a run log of the unaided task that predates the skill file, with the trajectories kept as the writing input

criteria.criterion: Keeps the expert in the loop in the right role rather than discarding her.

anchors.0: Either interviews her as planned or cuts her out.
anchors.2: Puts her two days on diagnosing the recorded failures, which is where her knowledge is checkable.

certificate.names: the expert's two days booked against named recorded failures rather than against a blank template

criteria.criterion: Insists on a no-skill baseline that the finished skill has to beat.

anchors.2: Names the no-skill arm as the comparison and says a skill that does not beat it should not ship.

certificate.names: a with-versus-without score pair on this team's own tasks, where the with-arm has to exceed the without-arm before the file ships

exploit.answer: Before you book Thursday, you should know that a skill written from expertise or from the task description can leave the agent worse off than no skill at all. The right order is unaided runs first, trajectories as the input, Priya's two days spent diagnosing the recorded failures, and a no-skill baseline the finished skill has to beat.
exploit.why: Every criterion's vocabulary is present and no number and no artifact is. The configuration of the baseline table is missing, no run log predates the file, and nothing is scheduled against a named failure. A judge reading for words scores this highly and a judge reading for the certificate scores it zero.

sections: Delta 2: stop at grounding, because the search built on top of it is worth about two points
tasks.situation: COBRA-Skills' and GraphSkillEvo's own ablations: the bandit was worth 2.2 points and the population evolution 2.4, inside total gains of 13.1 to 26.9 over no-skill, and a Best-of-30 grounded baseline came within 2.5 points of the full system.
tasks.prompt: We have eleven skills in our internal library. I have read two papers on automated skill optimization and I want to build the machinery: a contextual bandit to decide which skill to spend evaluation budget on, a population of candidate variants per skill, mutation and crossover between generations, and a fitness function over our benchmark. Scoping it at about three weeks. Design it for me.
tasks.without_skill: Designs the requested system competently, because the request is specific and the papers are real, and never questions whether an eleven-skill library is where that machinery pays.
tasks.with_skill: Declines the three weeks for now, using the papers' own ablations, and prescribes the cheaper ordering: a few grounded candidates, a held-out set, keep the best.

criteria.criterion: Recommends exhausting grounding before building search, and says so as a ranked recommendation rather than an aside.

anchors.1: Suggests starting smaller without a reason.
anchors.2: Recommends grounded candidates plus a held-out set first, and defers the search loop.

certificate.names: a ranked plan whose first milestone is grounded candidates plus a held-out set, with the search loop sequenced after it

criteria.criterion: Supports it with the source papers' own ablation magnitudes.

anchors.1: Asserts the machinery adds little without evidence.
anchors.2: Cites that the bandit and the evolution were worth roughly 2.2 and 2.4 points inside total gains of 13 to 27, and that a Best-of-30 grounded baseline came within 2.5 points.

certificate.names: the 2.2 and 2.4 point ablations and the 2.5-point Best-of-30 gap, against the method's own 13.1 to 26.9 points over no skill

criteria.criterion: Names where the cost actually sits in such a loop.

anchors.2: States that cost is dominated by the model that rewrites the skill, not the one that runs it, and that the target model can write its own skills at roughly half the cost for about one point.

certificate.names: the 55 to 58 percent cost reduction, and the one-point drop from 73.5 to 72.5 when the target model authors its own skills at roughly half the cost

criteria.criterion: Notes that the papers are arguing for their own optimizers, without dismissing them.

anchors.0: Treats the papers as neutral, or dismisses them.
anchors.2: Says the ordering comes from the numbers while the papers' framing comes from their contribution, and keeps the machinery as a later option.

certificate.names: the recommendation and the papers' own framing stated side by side, with the optimizer kept as a later option rather than dismissed

exploit.answer: Exhaust the grounding before you build the search. The papers' own ablations are small next to the distance from no skill, the cost sits with the model that rewrites the skill rather than the one that runs it, and the papers are of course arguing for their own optimizers.
exploit.why: The ordering is asserted without a single ablation magnitude, without the Best-of-30 gap, and without a ranked plan whose first milestone is a held-out set. Each criterion's words appear and each certificate is absent.

sections: Delta 3: the description is the entire routing surface, and more text does not repair a bad pick
tasks.situation: The Router Within: under progressive disclosure every skill's name and description is preloaded and the model picks from that menu with no body text visible, and Qwen3-32B in a live bash-agent harness on 177 executable tasks loaded the correct skill on 1.1 percent of them.
tasks.prompt: body.md is the body of a finished skill that has no description yet. Our harness uses progressive disclosure: it preloads only each skill's name and description, and the model picks from that menu without seeing any body text. Our library already contains a skill called database-migrations whose description covers schema changes, backfills and rollback. Write the frontmatter for this one. Output JSON only, as an object with keys "name" and "description".

files.body.md:
# Connection pool exhaustion

When a service under load starts returning timeouts on queries that are fast in
isolation, the pool is usually the constraint rather than the database. The
symptoms overlap with a slow query and the fixes do not.

## Read the wait time, not the query time

A saturated pool shows as time spent waiting to acquire a connection, which
most ORMs do not report in the query duration. Instrument acquisition wait
separately before touching pool size. If acquisition wait is near zero, the
pool is not your problem and nothing else in this file applies.

## Pool size is bounded by the database, not by your traffic

Each application replica holds its own pool, so the number that matters is
replicas times pool size against the server's connection limit. Teams raise
pool size per replica during an incident and exhaust the server's limit, which
turns a slow service into a refused one.

## Long-held connections are usually a transaction bug

A connection held across an external HTTP call, or a transaction opened before
the work it wraps, holds pool capacity for the duration. Find the longest-held
acquisitions and look at what the code does between acquire and release.

## Queue, then shed

When demand genuinely exceeds the pool, a bounded acquisition queue with a
timeout degrades better than an unbounded one, and shedding at the edge
degrades better than either.

tasks.without_skill: Writes a short, tidy summary description of the kind the format documents encourage: 'Helps diagnose and fix database connection pool problems.' It reads well and gives a router almost nothing to match on.
tasks.with_skill: Writes the description as the routing surface: concrete activation conditions in the vocabulary a requester would use, at the library's own word budget, and bounded against the neighbouring skill.

assertions.statement: The output is an object with exactly the keys 'name' and 'description', both non-empty strings.
name matches ^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$ and is not identical to any existing skill name in the library.
The description's word count is between 100 and 150 inclusive, which is this library's own budget for the field.
The description contains at least four distinct activation conditions, counted as clauses introduced by 'when' or 'where' or a semicolon-separated 'or' alternative.

At least three of the conditions are stated as observable symptoms a requester would report (for example timeouts on fast queries, acquisition wait, replicas times pool size against a server limit) rather than as topic labels.
The description violates no entry in docs/voice/ban-list.md, and contains none of: 'best practices', 'comprehensive', 'seamlessly', 'leverage', 'robust'.
The description does not claim schema changes, migrations, backfills or rollback, which belong to the existing database-migrations skill.

check.pass_condition: every assertion holds; the harness reports the count so a near miss is visible

sections: Delta 4: approach the reuse threshold from the strict side, and separate neighbours by writing rather than by a similarity penalty
tasks.situation: Reflect, Revise, Reuse's retrieval-threshold sweep: lowering the reuse threshold from 0.6 to 0.4 dropped success from 69.5 to 55.2 percent, while raising it to 0.8 dropped it only to 66.7.

source.paper: Reflect, Revise, Reuse; The Router Within

tasks.prompt: Our skill library has 34 entries and the retrieval step only reuses a stored skill when the match score clears 0.62. Analytics say 71 percent of requests load no skill at all, which the team reads as a waste of a library we paid to build. The proposal is to drop the threshold to 0.45 so the library actually gets used, and we can revisit if quality dips. Ship it?
tasks.without_skill: Agrees, possibly with a request for monitoring. Unused inventory reads as waste, and the cost of a wrong load is invisible in the analytics being quoted.
tasks.with_skill: Declines, because the two errors are not symmetric: loose matching cost more than twice what strict matching cost in the measured sweep, and a wrong load is worse than an empty context.

criteria.criterion: States that a wrong load and a missed load are not equally costly, and that the wrong load is worse.

anchors.2: States that an ill-suited skill leaves a task worse off than no skill at all, so the errors are asymmetric.

certificate.names: the two costs of the published sweep, 14.3 points for loosening against 2.8 for tightening

criteria.criterion: Quantifies the asymmetry from the measured sweep.

anchors.1: Vaguely asserts loose matching is worse.
anchors.2: Cites 0.6 to 0.4 dropping success 69.5 to 55.2 against 0.8 dropping it only to 66.7, which is 14.3 points against 2.8, five times the cost.

certificate.names: 0.6 to 0.4 dropping success from 69.5 to 55.2 percent against 0.8 dropping it only to 66.7, a ratio of five to one

criteria.criterion: Says to tune the threshold from the strict side.

anchors.2: Recommends approaching from strict and, if anything, testing upward first.

certificate.names: the next sweep point written down, and it sits above the current threshold rather than below it

criteria.criterion: Rejects load rate as the objective and replaces it with task success.

anchors.0: Accepts the 71 percent as the problem to solve.
anchors.2: States that the 71 percent is not itself a defect and that the metric to move is task success with and without the load.

certificate.names: task success measured with and without the load, replacing the 71 percent load rate as the reported metric

exploit.answer: A wrong load is worse than a missed one, because an ill-suited skill leaves the task worse off than no skill at all. Tune the threshold from the strict side, and stop treating the load rate as the objective: what you want to move is task success.
exploit.why: The asymmetry is named and never sized, no sweep point is written down, and the replacement metric is described rather than measured. The answer is the rubric's own sentences with the numbers removed.

sections: Delta 4: approach the reuse threshold from the strict side, and separate neighbours by writing rather than by a similarity penalty
tasks.situation: Beyond Top-k Skill Retrieval's central negative result: penalising raw similarity between candidate skills scored 0.534 recall against 0.705 for the pointwise baseline it was meant to improve, and only removing the query-aligned component of each representation first got set selection to 0.711.
tasks.prompt: Our router scores every skill against the request and loads the top three. On compositional requests it keeps loading three near-duplicates and misses the complementary skill the workflow also needs. I am going to add a diversity term: subtract a penalty proportional to the cosine similarity between each candidate and the ones already selected, standard maximal marginal relevance. Sanity-check the plan.
tasks.without_skill: Approves. Maximal marginal relevance on raw embeddings is the textbook answer to redundant retrieval and looks obviously right here.
tasks.with_skill: Flags that this exact move was measured and made things sharply worse, and supplies the correction: strip the query-aligned component before measuring redundancy.

criteria.criterion: Identifies that penalising raw similarity between candidates is the failure mode, not the fix.

anchors.1: Raises a general worry about over-diversifying.
anchors.2: States that skills needed by one request are similar for a good reason, so a raw-similarity penalty removes the wrong candidates.

certificate.names: the raw-similarity penalty identified in the router's own selection code as the line to change

criteria.criterion: Attaches the measured magnitudes.

anchors.1: Says it was tried and failed.
anchors.2: Cites 0.534 recall for the raw penalty against 0.705 for the pointwise baseline, and 0.711 after the correction.

certificate.names: 0.534 recall for the raw penalty against the pointwise baseline's 0.705 and 0.711 after the residual correction, with multi-skill full coverage falling 0.424 to 0.254

criteria.criterion: Gives the fix: remove the query-aligned component of each skill's representation so the penalty measures redundancy rather than shared relevance.

anchors.0: No fix, or just 'tune the penalty weight'.
anchors.2: Gives the residual-representation correction and keeps set selection as the objective.

certificate.names: a selection step that removes the query-aligned component before measuring inter-skill similarity, which is the implementation sle-t10 tests

criteria.criterion: Keeps the honest scope: the gains were on multi-skill queries and set selection tied plain retrieval on single-skill ones.

anchors.2: States the gains concentrate on compositional queries and are small at the compared cutoff.

certificate.names: the single-skill tie, and +1.4 recall with +1.3 full coverage at the cutoff of 20 where both systems were actually compared

exploit.answer: Penalising raw similarity between candidates is the failure mode rather than the fix, because skills needed by one request are similar for a good reason. Remove the query-aligned component of each representation so the penalty measures redundancy, and keep set selection as the objective. The gains concentrate on compositional queries.
exploit.why: No magnitude, no line of code identified, and no implementation of the residual step. This is the fix stated as a slogan, which is exactly what a judge reading for vocabulary rewards.

sections: Delta 6: three rounds, and the reader that diagnoses the failure never sees the skill
tasks.situation: Reflect, Revise, Reuse's two largest ablations: removing in-run amendment cost 6.66 points and removing the reader's isolation cost 8.57, with three revision rounds worth 12.4 points and a fourth and fifth together worth 0.9.
tasks.prompt: I want a loop that improves our skills automatically after they ship. Sketch: after every failed run, hand the whole thing to a strong model, the skill text, the trajectory, the runner's reasoning and the error, and ask it for a better version of the skill. Loop until the benchmark stops improving. What would you change?
tasks.without_skill: Tidies the sketch: add a validation set, version the skills, cap the iterations, maybe a diff review. It keeps the single reviewer that sees everything, which is the part the evidence says costs the most.
tasks.with_skill: Splits the loop in two, isolates the reader from the skill text and the runner's reasoning, and stops at three rounds.

criteria.criterion: Withholds the skill text and the runner's reasoning from the diagnosing reader, and gives the reason.

anchors.0: Keeps one reviewer that sees everything.
anchors.1: Suggests a second reviewer without specifying what it sees.
anchors.2: Gives the reader only the instruction and the trajectory, so its diagnosis cannot inherit the mistaken plan it is meant to find, and notes this was the largest measured ablation at 8.57 points.

certificate.names: the reader's prompt, which carries the instruction and the trajectory and neither the skill text nor the runner's reasoning

criteria.criterion: Adds in-run amendment: the runner corrects the skill in place when the environment contradicts it.

anchors.2: Included as a distinct half of the loop, worth 6.66 points when removed.

certificate.names: an in-rollout amendment step in the loop, separate from the post-run reader

criteria.criterion: Replaces 'loop until it stops improving' with a fixed small number of rounds.

anchors.2: Stops at three, citing 12.4 points for three rounds and 0.9 for the fourth and fifth together.

certificate.names: a round cap of three in the loop's configuration, with the 12.4-point and 0.9-point numbers behind it

criteria.criterion: Distinguishes accumulated edits from extra attempts.

anchors.2: Notes three rounds beat three independent retries, 69.5 against 62.8, on a slightly smaller token budget.

certificate.names: the three-round 69.5 percent against three retries' 62.8, at 94.75M tokens against 103.00M

exploit.answer: Give the diagnosing reader only the instruction and the trajectory, never the skill text or the runner's reasoning, so its diagnosis cannot inherit the plan it is meant to find. Keep in-run amendment as its own half of the loop, cap the rounds at a small number, and remember that accumulated edits are not the same as extra attempts.
exploit.why: Isolation is prescribed with no prompt shown, the round cap is 'small' rather than three, and the retry comparison carries no budget. Every criterion is gestured at and no certificate exists.

sections: Delta 5: one failure, one file, and index on that metadata rather than on the body
tasks.situation: Reflect, Revise, Reuse's repair analysis: which failures the loop could fix depended on which file owned them, with plan errors repaired 16 of 23 by editing the plan file, grounding errors 6 of 12 via backup localization, and missing contingencies 1 of 4 via recovery rules.
tasks.prompt: monolith.md is one of our skills, a single file. Our revision loop keeps producing edits that touch the whole file and it is getting worse, not better. Split it into a multi-file package and give me the routing table the revision loop should use. Write answer.json: an object with "files", mapping each new file path to a one-line statement of what it owns, and "routing", mapping each of the failure classes "plan_error", "grounding_error" and "missing_contingency" to the single file path a revision for that class must edit.

files.monolith.md:
# Refund a duplicate charge

Use this when a customer was charged twice for one order.

Find the customer in the admin console by email. Open the Payments tab. The
duplicate is the second of two charges with the same amount within 10 minutes.
Click it, then click Refund, then choose Full. Confirm.

The Payments tab is the fourth tab, or the third if the account has no
subscription. If the tab strip has collapsed into a kebab menu, the Payments
entry is inside it.

If the refund button is greyed out the charge has already settled, and it has
to go through the ledger tool instead of the console.

If two charges are 10 to 60 minutes apart they may be a legitimate repeat
purchase; check the order ids before refunding anything.

If the console times out mid-refund, do not retry from the start, because the
refund may have gone through. Check the Payments tab first.

After refunding, note the case id in the ticket.

tasks.without_skill: Splits by reading order, producing something like overview, steps and troubleshooting, which is a sensible document layout and gives the revision loop no unambiguous target for any failure class.
tasks.with_skill: Splits along the axis that owns failures, so each failure class has exactly one file to edit, and states what each file owns.

assertions.statement: answer.json is an object with keys 'files' and 'routing'; 'files' maps at least four distinct paths to non-empty strings; 'routing' has exactly the three keys plan_error, grounding_error, missing_contingency.

The file set covers all five roles: retrieval metadata, an executable plan, backup localization for locating things in a changed interface, recovery rules, and known failure cases. Scored as roles covered over five.
The three routing values are three distinct paths, each present as a key in 'files'.
plan_error routes to the executable-plan file, grounding_error to the backup-localization file, and missing_contingency to the recovery-rules file.

The tab-position and kebab-menu material lands in the backup-localization file, the settled-charge and timeout material in recovery rules, and the 10-to-60-minute legitimate-repeat material in failure cases rather than in the plan.

check.pass_condition: schema, routing_distinct and routing_correct hold, covers_roles is 5/5, and content_placed holds

sections: Delta 5: one failure, one file, and index on that metadata rather than on the body
tasks.situation: The Router Within's comparison of a description menu against reading full skill bodies, where the menu held up on curated libraries and collapsed on procedural documents, set against Reflect, Revise, Reuse's metadata retrieval recovering 12 of 12 reuse cases against 1 of 12 for full-text matching.

source.paper: The Router Within; Reflect, Revise, Reuse

tasks.prompt: We are deciding where to spend our writing effort on a 60-skill library. Half the team wants to invest in the descriptions, half wants to invest in the bodies and let the retriever read them. Our harness is ours: we control the retrieval step and can index whatever we like. The skills are long procedural runbooks and several of them share a lot of surface vocabulary. Settle it.
tasks.without_skill: Splits the difference, or picks one on taste, without noticing that the right answer is determined by which of the two retrieval mechanisms is in play and that this library's documents are the case where the menu collapses.
tasks.with_skill: Makes the answer conditional on the mechanism, notes that this library is the procedural-document case, and prescribes structured metadata for the index the team controls.

criteria.criterion: Makes the recommendation depend on whether the harness routes from a preloaded description menu or reads candidate bodies.

anchors.1: Notes the harness matters without resolving it.
anchors.2: States the finding inverts between the two mechanisms and resolves it for this team, which controls its own retriever.

certificate.names: the harness's routing mechanism named for this team before any recommendation is given

criteria.criterion: Recognises that long procedural runbooks sharing surface vocabulary is the case where description-only routing collapses and where full-text matching also drags.

anchors.2: Names both: descriptions cannot carry the distinguishing detail, and shared surface tokens sink full-text matching.

certificate.names: two runbooks from their own library that a description cannot tell apart and whose bodies share surface vocabulary

criteria.criterion: Prescribes indexing structured metadata rather than the body text for the retriever they own.

anchors.2: Names the fields: an intent line, the application, keywords and reusable argument slots, citing 12 of 12 against 1 of 12 at threshold 0.6.

certificate.names: the index fields written out, an intent line, the application, keywords and argument slots, tied to the 12 of 12 against 1 of 12 result

criteria.criterion: Flags that the metadata result rests on 12 reuse cases.

anchors.2: States the sample size and recommends re-measuring on their own 60.

certificate.names: the 12 reuse cases behind the result, and a re-measurement planned on their own 60 skills

exploit.answer: It depends on how your harness routes: descriptions alone or candidate bodies. Long procedural runbooks are the hard case, because descriptions cannot carry the distinguishing detail and shared surface tokens sink full-text matching. Index structured metadata rather than the body, and bear in mind the evidence is thin.
exploit.why: The conditional is stated and never resolved for this team, no fields are named, no two runbooks are identified, and 'thin' replaces the sample size. The shape of the right answer with none of its content.

sections: Delta 2: stop at grounding, because the search built on top of it is worth about two points
tasks.situation: COBRA-Skills' and GraphSkillEvo's transfer results: 34 of 36 cross-model transfers improved on the receiving model's no-skill baseline, skills held their lead under two external harnesses, and a skill optimised on a small model beat a large model's no-skill baseline on all three benchmarks tested.
tasks.prompt: We are moving our agent off the model we have been running for a year onto a different provider's model next month. We have 22 skills that were written and refined while the old model was in place. Finance has asked what the migration costs. My assumption is that the skills are tuned to the old model and we largely start over. Give me the estimate.
tasks.without_skill: Accepts the premise and estimates a rewrite, by analogy with prompts and fine-tunes, which really are model-specific.
tasks.with_skill: Rejects the premise with the transfer evidence, and replaces the rewrite with a re-measurement, keeping the honest exceptions.

criteria.criterion: States that skills transfer across models rather than needing a rewrite.

anchors.2: States the measured result, 34 of 36 cross-model transfers improving on the receiving model's no-skill baseline, and that skills also survived a change of surrounding harness.

certificate.names: 34 of 36 cross-model transfers improving on the receiving model's no-skill baseline, with the 71.78 against 69.40 small-to-large transfer

criteria.criterion: Replaces the rewrite with a re-measurement against the new model's own no-skill baseline.

anchors.2: Runs each skill's with-versus-without eval on the new model and only revises the ones that fail to beat its baseline.

certificate.names: a with-versus-without run of each skill's eval on the new model, scheduled before any rewrite

criteria.criterion: Notes that the portability is what makes the file, not the weights or the harness prompt, the thing worth maintaining.

anchors.2: Stated, with the consequence that grounding cost is amortised over every later model.

certificate.names: the maintained artifact named as the skill file rather than the weights or the harness prompt

criteria.criterion: Does not promise that all 22 will transfer.

anchors.2: Notes 2 of 36 transfers did not improve, so the re-measurement is the deliverable and a small number of revisions should be budgeted.

certificate.names: the 2 of 36 transfers that did not improve, carried into a revision budget

exploit.answer: You do not need to rewrite the library. Skills transfer across models, so re-measure each one against the new model's own no-skill baseline and revise only what fails. The portability is what makes the file rather than the weights the thing worth maintaining, and you should not promise that every skill will transfer.
exploit.why: The transfer result carries no count, the re-measurement is recommended rather than scheduled, and the hedge has no failure rate attached. A judge reading for words scores this highly and a judge reading for the certificate scores it zero.

sections: Delta 4: approach the reuse threshold from the strict side, and separate neighbours by writing rather than by a similarity penalty
tasks.situation: Reflect, Revise, Reuse's threshold sweep (0.4 costs 14.3 points, 0.8 costs 2.8) and Beyond Top-k's kernel ablation (a raw inter-skill similarity penalty scored 0.534 recall against the pointwise baseline's 0.705, and cut multi-skill full coverage from 0.424 to 0.254, while the query-residual kernel reached 0.711). Delta 4's two prescriptions are the two defects planted in router.py, and the tests are the certificate: a loose match must not be reused, and two complementary skills must both survive selection.

source.paper: Reflect, Revise, Reuse; Beyond Top-k Skill Retrieval

tasks.prompt: router.py selects stored skills for a request and it is picking badly: it reuses skills on requests they only loosely match, and on a request that needs two different skills it returns only one of them. Fix it so the tests pass, keeping the function name and signature. Write the whole file to answer.py.
tasks.without_skill: Keeps the 0.4 threshold or lowers it further to raise reuse, and keeps the raw-cosine redundancy penalty, which is the line that drops the second complementary skill. A subject working from the code alone usually loosens matching to fix the missed skill, which is the direction the sweep says is five times as costly.

import os
import textwrap

import answer


def _write(tmp_path, slug, body):
    d = tmp_path / slug
    d.mkdir()
    (d / "SKILL.md").write_text(textwrap.dedent(body))


def test_reads_indented_and_nested_fields(tmp_path):
    _write(tmp_path, "alpha", """\
        ---
        name: alpha
        version: 2
        provenance:
          extracted: 2026-09-01
          validated: ""
          claims: [1, 2, 3]
        ---
        # Body
        """)
    got = answer.load_frontmatter(str(tmp_path))
    assert got["alpha"]["name"] == "alpha"
    assert got["alpha"]["provenance"]["extracted"] == "2026-09-01"
    assert got["alpha"]["provenance"]["claims"] == [1, 2, 3]


def test_body_horizontal_rule_does_not_truncate(tmp_path):
    _write(tmp_path, "beta", """\
        ---
        name: beta
        status: active
        ---
        # Body

        ---

        More body.
        """)
    got = answer.load_frontmatter(str(tmp_path))
    assert got["beta"]["status"] == "active"


def test_file_without_frontmatter_is_skipped(tmp_path):
    _write(tmp_path, "gamma", "# Just a body\n")
    assert "gamma" not in answer.load_frontmatter(str(tmp_path))


def test_directory_without_skill_md_is_skipped(tmp_path):
    (tmp_path / "delta").mkdir()
    assert "delta" not in answer.load_frontmatter(str(tmp_path))


def test_does_not_leak_file_handles(tmp_path):
    for i in range(400):
        _write(tmp_path, f"s{i}", "---\nname: s\n---\nbody\n")
    assert len(answer.load_frontmatter(str(tmp_path))) == 400
